dervis-irab:5-7.t:
* Vocabulary:
(النطفة): the fluid of the man or the woman; the plural is نطاف and نطف. It is what is known as المني (semen), on the pattern of فني, and المنيّ on the pattern of إليّ, and المنية on the pattern of رمية; it is pluralised as منى on the pattern of قفل.
منى, أمنى and منّى have one and the same meaning. النطفة is also clear water, whether little or much. More will be said about it later.
(عَلَقَةٍ): العلقة is congealed blood, which is what is meant here; also that which clings to the hand, anything that is hung up, the tree foliage on which livestock subsist, and a small black creature that sucks blood (the leech); the plural is علق.
(مُضْغَةٍ): a lump of flesh the size of what is chewed.
(مُخَلَّقَةٍ): المخلّقة is that which is fashioned evenly, smooth, free of deficiency and defect. One says خلّق السواك والعود (he shaped the tooth-stick and the rod) when he made it even and smoothed it, from their expression صخرة خلقاء (a smooth rock). It is as though Allah the Exalted creates the lumps of flesh differing and varied: some of them are complete in form and smooth of defects, and some of them are the opposite of that; and according to that variation the created beings vary in their forms and makeup.
(طِفْلًا): الطفل with a kasra on the ṭāʾ is applied to the child from the time of separation (birth) until the time of puberty. As for الطَّفل with a fatḥa, it means soft and delicate, and a woman is طفلة. As for الطَّفَل with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ and the fāʾ, it is the time after the afternoon (ʿaṣr), from their expression طفلت الشمس when the sun inclines to setting. أطفلت المرأة means the woman came to have a child. In al-Mukhtār: الطفل is used as singular and plural; in the hadith, he ﷺ was asked about أطفال المشركين (the children of the polytheists). In al-Asās and al-Lisān, the gist of what is said is: he is a طفل, clearly in childhood (بيّن الطفولة); he did that in his childhood (طفولته); a woman and a doe are مطفل (having young); and طفّلت ولدها: she reared her child. Al-Akhṭal said, describing clouds:
إذا زعزعته الريح جرّ ذيولها ... كما زحفت عوذ ثقال تطفّل
(When the wind shakes it, it drags its trains, as heavy she-camels with newborn young creep along, tending their little ones.)
And a woman is طفلة, and طفلة الأنامل: soft (of fingertips); and بنان طفل: soft fingertips. Dhū al-Rumma said:
أسيلة مستنّ الوشاحين قانىء ... بأطرافها الحناء في سبط طفل
(Smooth where the two sashes run, the henna deep red on her fingertips, on soft, slender fingers.)
And طفل (it became soft), طفولة and طفالة. And "I will come to him في طفل الغداة and طفل العشي", that is, shortly after sunrise and shortly before sunset. The poet said:
باكرتها طفل الغداة بغارة ... والمبتغون خطار ذاك قليل
(I came upon them early, at the first light of morning, with a raid, and those who seek such a risk are few.)
And Labīd said:
فتدليت عليه قافلا ... وعلى الأرض غيابات الطّفل
(So I descended upon it on my way back, while the shadows of dusk lay upon the earth.)
And طفّلت الشمس when it drew near to setting; طفّل الليل: the night approached and cast its shadow; طفّل علينا and تطفّل (he came uninvited), and he is a طفيلي (a sponger). You say: "He kept sponging on people until he eclipsed Ṭufayl al-Aʿrās" — he was a man from Kufa to whom sponging (التطفيل) was attributed.
(أشده): it was discussed earlier, and we say here: الأشد is the perfection of strength [Translator's note: the printed text reads القول ("speech"); القوة ("strength") seems intended], intellect and discernment. It is one of the plural words for which no singular is used, and it is between thirty and forty.
(هامِدَةً): الهمود is stillness and subsidence; همدت الأرض: the earth dried up and became effaced; همد الثوب: the garment wore out.
(اهْتَزَّتْ): it moved; it is used here figuratively for the earth's bringing forth its plants by means of the water.
(رَبَتْ): it increased and rose, from ربا يربو.

* I'rab:
(يا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ فِي رَيْبٍ مِنَ الْبَعْثِ فَإِنَّا خَلَقْناكُمْ مِنْ تُرابٍ): the i'rab of يا أيها الناس has preceded. إن is conditional; كنتم is a deficient (nāqiṣ) past verb, the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), and the tāʾ is its noun; في ريب is its khabar (predicate); من البعث is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted naʿt (adjective) of ريب. فإنا: the fāʾ links (the apodosis), and إنّ with its noun; the clause خلقناكم is its khabar; من تراب is attached to خلقناكم. His saying فإنا خلقناكم was permitted to occur as an apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) only by interpreting it as: "then what removes your doubt is that you look at the beginning of your creation."
(ثُمَّ مِنْ نُطْفَةٍ ثُمَّ مِنْ عَلَقَةٍ ثُمَّ مِنْ مُضْغَةٍ مُخَلَّقَةٍ وَغَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ): it is conjoined with ثم to indicate an interval of time in the development of creation and its gradual progression from state to state. His saying مخلقة is a naʿt of مضغة, and غير مخلقة is conjoined to مخلقة. What is meant is a detailed account of the state of the lump of flesh: that at first it is a piece in which none of the limbs is visible, then after that they appear little by little.
(لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ وَنُقِرُّ فِي الْأَرْحامِ ما نَشاءُ إِلى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى): لنبين: the lām is for causation (taʿlīl), and نبين is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after the lām of causation; the lām with what follows it is attached to خلقناكم. Or the lām is for outcome and consequence (al-ṣayrūra wa-l-ʿāqiba), that is: through these acts of His there becomes clear, of His power and knowledge, what cannot be fathomed or encompassed; that is why the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of نبين was omitted. That is in order to argue from this power that whoever is able to begin creation is able to repeat it, so there is no room for denial and no ground for doubt. ونقر: the wāw is resumptive, and نقر is a nominative imperfect verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "we"; في الأرحام is attached to نقر; ما is a mafʿūl bihi, and the clause نشاء is its ṣila (relative clause); إلى أجل مسمى is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial). It was made a new sentence only because the meaning is not "We created you in order to settle." مسمى is a naʿt of أجل حرف [Translator's note: the word حرف appears thus in the printed text and seems out of place], that is, (a term) whose time of emergence is extended.
(ثُمَّ نُخْرِجُكُمْ طِفْلًا ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوا أَشُدَّكُمْ): ثم is a conjunction with interval also; نخرجكم is conjoined to نقر; the agent of نخرجكم is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "we", and the kāf is a mafʿūl bihi; طفلا is a ḥāl from the object of نخرجكم. ثم لتبلغوا: a verb must be supplied, namely نعمّركم (We give you long life). لتبلغوا: the lām is for causation or for outcome, and تبلغوا is accusative by an implied أن after the lām; the wāw is the agent, and أشدكم is a mafʿūl bihi.
(وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُتَوَفَّى وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ): the wāw is a conjunction; منكم is a fronted khabar and من a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject), and the clause يتوفى is the ṣila; منكم is a fronted khabar and من a postponed mubtadaʾ, and the clause يرد is the ṣila; إلى أرذل العمر is attached to يرد. To ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is attributed the saying that the most decrepit age is seventy-five years; it is said eighty; Qatāda said ninety. The correct view is that it is senility and dotage, and man's reaching the stage of exhaustion and feebleness, or reverting to the stage of childhood, weak in body and mind, dull of understanding.
(لِكَيْلا يَعْلَمَ مِنْ بَعْدِ عِلْمٍ شَيْئاً): لكيلا is attached to يرد; يعلم is accusative by an implied أن after the lām, and كي is maṣdar-forming [Translator's note: the author says يعلم is made accusative by an implied أن while also calling كي maṣdar-forming; as written]; من بعد علم is attached to an omitted ḥāl, because علم has the sense of عرف (to know); شيئا is the mafʿūl bihi of يعلم.
(وَتَرَى الْأَرْضَ هامِدَةً فَإِذا أَنْزَلْنا عَلَيْهَا الْماءَ اهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ وَأَنْبَتَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ زَوْجٍ بَهِيجٍ): this sentence is resumptive, set out to establish the second proof. For the first proof includes what is seen and witnessed and what is not so, and so it was expressed with "creation"; whereas this proof falls within the scope of sight and is included in the class of visible things, and so it was expressed by His saying وترى (and you see). الأرض is a mafʿūl bihi, and هامدة is a ḥāl from الأرض. فإذا: the fāʾ is a conjunction, and إذا is a future adverb of time containing the sense of condition; the clause أنزلنا is in a genitive construct with the adverb; عليها is attached to أنزلنا; الماء is a mafʿūl bihi; the clause اهتزت has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of a non-jussivising condition; ربت is conjoined to اهتزت, and likewise His saying وأنبتت. من كل زوج is a naʿt of an omitted mafʿūl bihi, that is, things and kinds being of every kind; بهيج is a naʿt of زوج.
(ذلِكَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ الْحَقُّ وَأَنَّهُ يُحْيِ الْمَوْتى وَأَنَّهُ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ): ذلك is a mubtadaʾ and بأن الله is the khabar. It is also said that ذلك is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "the matter is that", in which case the bāʾ with what follows it is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl. أنّ with its noun; هو is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl) or a mubtadaʾ; الحق is the khabar of أنّ or the khabar of هو, and the second mubtadaʾ with its khabar is the khabar of أنّ. وأنه is conjoined to بأن: أنّ with its noun, and the clause يحيي الموتى is its khabar. وأنه على كل شيء قدير is also conjoined. There is no harm here in citing a remark of Abū Ḥayyān, the gist of which is that the bāʾ is not causal, but rather attached to an omitted element, its implied form being "bearing witness that" (شاهد بأن); and this applies to the two aspects we mentioned above.
(وَأَنَّ السَّاعَةَ آتِيَةٌ لا رَيْبَ فِيها): وأن الساعة is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "and the matter is that the Hour…". أنّ with its noun, and آتية is its khabar; لا is the lā of generic negation, ريب is its noun and فيها its khabar; the clause is a ḥāl, or a second khabar of أنّ.
(وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَبْعَثُ مَنْ فِي الْقُبُورِ): conjoined to what precedes. أنّ with its noun, and the clause يبعث is its khabar; من is a mafʿūl bihi, and في القبور is attached to an omitted element that is the ṣila of من.

* Rhetoric:
In the saying of the Exalted «وَتَرَى الْأَرْضَ هامِدَةً فَإِذا أَنْزَلْنا عَلَيْهَا الْماءَ اهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ وَأَنْبَتَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ زَوْجٍ بَهِيجٍ» there are rhetorical arts which the breadth of this book can hardly accommodate; we will try to summarise them as far as possible. The first of them is:

1- The combination of ṭibāq (antithesis) and takāfuʾ (equivalence):
Because one of the two opposites or one of the two counterparts comes literally and the other figuratively. The stillness of the earth (همود) and its stirring (اهتزاز) are opposites, because همود is stillness, and اهتزاز here is a particular movement, and both are figurative. Rising (الربو) and sprouting (الإنبات) are opposites, and both are literal. We said this only because the earth swells at the time the water falls upon it and does not sprout in that state; then, when the supply from the sky is cut off and the air dries the moisture of the water, the swelling subsides and the earth returns to its level state, cracks and sprouts. So the beginning of the verse is takāfuʾ, and what corresponds to it at its end is ṭibāq.
2- Irdāf (using a consequent term):
Along with these two arts it also contains the art of irdāf, which is, as Qudāma mentioned in Naqd al-Shiʿr, that the speaker intends a meaning but does not express it with the word coined for it, nor with an allusive word indicating many meanings, but with a word that is the "follower" (ردف) and consequent of the particular meaning, close to the word for the particular meaning as the rider behind is close to the rider. It was referred to earlier in (Sūrat) Hūd. Here in this verse He turned away from the literal words "movement" and "stillness" to their consequents, the words همود and اهتزاز, because the consequent words fit the intended meaning: for همود is used to mean death, and the earth, in its state of being idle without watering and vegetation, is dead land (موات), so turning to the word همود, by which death is expressed, was more fitting than the word "stillness". And the figurative اهتزاز suggests liveliness [Translator's note: the printed text reads بالعطالة ("idleness"); the context suggests liveliness or giving], like the stirring of the one praised at praise. For that reason He turned from the general word for movement to the particular word for movement, because it suggests that the earth, when watered, will give of its vegetation what pleases, by treating its watering as something that delights it, so it stirred to signal giving. Thus the benefit of turning to the consequent word has become clear, for the meanings it gives which the literal word does not give.

3- Tahdhīb (refinement):
The composition of this verse, along with what it contains of takāfuʾ, ṭibāq, irdāf and iʾtilāf, came marked by tahdhīb, because of the excellent ordering in it: the word اهتزاز precedes the word ربو, and the word ربو precedes إنبات. For when the water descends on the earth it separates its particles and enters between them; and the separation of the particles of inanimate substances is their movement at the time of the breaking of contact, because the division of a substance indicates the movement of its two parts, or one of them, from its place, and movement means nothing but this. So اهتزاز must be mentioned right after the watering, just as ربو came after اهتزاز: for when water enters soil, it rises relative to its state before that, and this is exactly ربو. It has already been explained that sprouting occurs only after the swelling and the drying of the water's moisture and the return of the soil to its state and its cracking. Thus tahdhīb is achieved in the composition of this verse through excellent ordering, and joined with that is excellent sequence, since everything that ought to be conjoined-to precedes everything that ought to be conjoined.

4- Al-madhhab al-kalāmī (the dialectical method):
In the saying of the Exalted from the beginning of Sūrat al-Ḥajj up to His saying «وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَبْعَثُ مَنْ فِي الْقُبُورِ» there is the art of al-madhhab al-kalāmī. For in these verses there are five conclusions drawn from ten premises; they are set out in detail in order:
a- The saying of the Exalted «ذلِكَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ الْحَقُّ»: that is because it has been established for us by mass-transmitted (mutawātir) report that He, Glorified is He, informed of the quaking of the Hour, magnifying it; and that is certain in its truth, because it is a report reported by one whose truthfulness is established, from One whose power is established, transmitted to us by mass transmission, so it is true (ḥaqq); and none informs truly of what will be except the Truth (al-Ḥaqq); so Allah is the Truth.
b- He, Glorified is He, informed that He gives life to the dead, because the Exalted informed of the terrors of the Hour as He informed, and the attainment of the benefit of this report depends on the dead being brought to life so that they witness those terrors which He, Glorified is He, has made for their sake. And it has been established that He has power over all things, and among things is giving life to the dead; so He gives life to the dead.
c- And He informed that He has power over all things, because He informed that whoever follows the devils and whoever disputes about Him without knowledge, He will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze, and none is able to do that except one who has power over all things; so He has power over all things.
d- And He informed that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, because He informed with truthful report that He created man from dust, up to His saying «لِكَيْلا يَعْلَمَ مِنْ بَعْدِ عِلْمٍ شَيْئاً», and He, Glorified is He, struck a likeness for that with the lifeless earth upon which water descends, so it stirs, swells and grows every delightful kind. And He created man as He informed: He brought him into existence by creation, then caused him not to exist by death, then will restore him by resurrection; and He brought the earth into existence after non-existence, gave it life by creation, then caused it to die by drought, then gave it life by fertility. And His report in all of that has proved true, by the evidence of the witnessed reality for the absent expected thing, until the report turned into eyewitness; His report is true.
e- In the coming of the Hour: and the Hour does not come except with the raising of those in the graves, since it is an expression for a period in which the dead rise for requital. So the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and He, Glorified is He, will raise those in the graves.

5- Majāz (figurative usage):
In the saying of the Exalted «وَأَنْبَتَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ زَوْجٍ بَهِيجٍ», He attributed sprouting to the earth, and this is a rational (ʿaqlī) majāz, because the one who causes growth in reality is Allah the Exalted. The discussion of majāz has preceded more than once, and we add here that majāz is the opposite of ḥaqīqa (literal usage). Ḥaqīqa is of the pattern faʿīla in the sense of mafʿūla, from أحقّ الأمر يحقّه when he established it, or from حققته when you were certain of it. The opposite of majāz was called by that name only because it is something established and known through indication. And majāz is of the pattern mafʿal from جاز الشيء يجوزه when he passed beyond it; so when the word is turned away from what the original coinage of the language requires, it is described as majāz, meaning that they took it beyond its original place, or it passed beyond the place in which it was first coined.

The two conditions of majāz:
Majāz exists only with two conditions:
a- That the word be transferred from a meaning for which the word was first coined. By this it is distinguished from the homonymous word and from a lie that is claimed to be majāz.
b- The second condition is that the transfer be due to an affinity and connection between the origin and the branch. For that reason transferred proper names are not described as majāz; an example of that is your naming a man "Stone" (الحجر): it is said that this is majāz, and although you have transferred the name "stone" to the human being, it is a transfer for no affinity, since there is no affinity between the reality of stone and the reality of man. Whenever these two conditions are realised in a word, that word is majāz.

The two kinds of majāz:
Majāz is of two kinds: majāz of istiʿāra (metaphor) and majāz of ḥadhf (ellipsis). The first is based on simile (tashbīh), because it is making a thing (stand) for a thing for exaggeration in the simile, as in your saying "I met a lion", meaning that you met a brave man; but there is no transfer in it, as preceded, and a fuller exposition of this topic will come. So in the saying of the Exalted «وَأَنْبَتَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ زَوْجٍ بَهِيجٍ», He transferred sprouting to the earth and made its greenness, freshness, abundant herbage and wondrous colours belong to it, whereas in reality all of that belongs to Allah.

dervis-irab:8-13.t:
* Vocabulary:
(ثانِيَ عِطْفِهِ): الثني is twisting. In al-Qāmūs: ثنى يثني الشيء means he bent it, folded it, turned part of it back onto part, and held it back. العطف is the side, which a person bends, twists and inclines when turning away from something; it is an expression by which arrogance is meant.
(حَرْفٍ): an edge; the detail of its meaning will come in the Rhetoric section.

* I'rab:
(وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يُجادِلُ فِي اللَّهِ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ وَلا هُدىً وَلا كِتابٍ مُنِيرٍ): ومن الناس من يجادل في الله بغير علم: the discussion of it has preceded in detail, so refresh your memory of it. ولا هدى is conjoined to علم, and ولا كتاب منير is also conjoined. The discussion of the repetition of this verse will come in the Rhetoric section.
(ثانِيَ عِطْفِهِ لِيُضِلَّ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ): ثاني is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of يجادل. It is made accusative as a ḥāl — though a condition of the ḥāl is that it be indefinite — only because its annexation is with the intention of separation, and the nunation is intended as though pronounced. عطفه is the muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct); the "bending of the side" will be discussed in the Rhetoric section. ليضل: the lām is for causation (taʿlīl), or for outcome and consequence (al-ʿāqiba wa-l-ṣayrūra) — and perhaps this is preferable as it suits the context; يضل is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after the lām, and the agent is latent, its implied form being "he"; عن سبيل الله is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) يضل, that is, from His religion.
(لَهُ فِي الدُّنْيا خِزْيٌ وَنُذِيقُهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ عَذابَ الْحَرِيقِ): له is a fronted khabar (predicate); في الدنيا is a ḥāl, because it was a naʿt (adjective) of خزي and was placed before it, according to the well-known rule; خزي is a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject). ونذيقه: the wāw is a conjunction, and نذيقه is a verb, a latent agent and a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); يوم القيامة is an adverb of time attached (to it); عذاب الحريق is a second mafʿūl bihi. The clause له في الدنيا is a ḥāl.
(ذلِكَ بِما قَدَّمَتْ يَداكَ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ لَيْسَ بِظَلَّامٍ لِلْعَبِيدِ): ذلك is a mubtadaʾ and بما is the khabar; the clause قدمت is the ṣila (relative clause), and يداك is the agent. وأن is conjoined to قدمت [Translator's note: as written; it is conjoined to ما], so it is in the position of genitive; أنّ with its noun, and the clause ليس is its khabar; the noun of ليس is latent, its implied form being "he"; the bāʾ is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition, and ظلام is a noun genitive in form and accusative in position, the khabar of ليس; للعبيد is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to ظلام. The clause ذلك بما قدمت يداك is the speech-object of an omitted verb of saying, and the clause of saying is a ḥāl.
(وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَعْبُدُ اللَّهَ عَلى حَرْفٍ): the wāw is a conjunction or resumptive; the sentence is resumptive, set out to explain the state of those wavering in their faith and doubting their religion. من الناس is a fronted khabar; من is an indefinite qualified noun (nakira mawṣūfa), and it is a postponed mubtadaʾ, that is, qualified by an anxious worship that is neither settled nor firm, so it is exposed to whims, and the least trial or harm that befalls them blows it away. The clause يعبد الله is a naʿt of من; على حرف is a ḥāl from the agent of يعبد, that is, unsteady and wobbling. Further explanation of this expression will come in the Rhetoric section.
(فَإِنْ أَصابَهُ خَيْرٌ اطْمَأَنَّ بِهِ وَإِنْ أَصابَتْهُ فِتْنَةٌ انْقَلَبَ عَلى وَجْهِهِ خَسِرَ الدُّنْيا وَالْآخِرَةَ): فإن: the fāʾ is a conjunction and إن is conditional; أصابه is a past verb in the position of jussive (majzūm) as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); the hāʾ is a mafʿūl bihi and خير is the agent; اطمأن is a past verb in the position of jussive as the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ); به is attached to اطمأن. وإن: the wāw conjoins to the first إن; أصابته فتنة is conjoined to what preceded; انقلب is the apodosis; على وجهه is also a ḥāl; the clause خسر الدنيا والآخرة is also a ḥāl from the agent of انقلب, and you may make it a resumptive clause or make it a badal (substitute) of the clause انقلب على وجهه. الدنيا is the object of خسر, and الآخرة is conjoined to الدنيا.
(ذلِكَ هُوَ الْخُسْرانُ الْمُبِينُ): ذلك is a mubtadaʾ, هو is a second mubtadaʾ, and الخسران is the khabar of هو; the clause is the khabar of ذلك; المبين is a naʿt of الخسران; the sentence is resumptive. You may make هو a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl).
(يَدْعُوا مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ ما لا يَضُرُّهُ وَما لا يَنْفَعُهُ ذلِكَ هُوَ الضَّلالُ الْبَعِيدُ): this clause may be a ḥāl from the agent of يعبد, and it may be resumptive. يدعو is an imperfect verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; من دون الله is a ḥāl; ما is a relative noun, a mafʿūl bihi; لا is negating, and the clause لا يضره is the ṣila; وما لا ينفعه is conjoined to the previous clause. The i'rab of the like of ذلك هو الضلال البعيد has preceded.
(يَدْعُوا لَمَنْ ضَرُّهُ أَقْرَبُ مِنْ نَفْعِهِ لَبِئْسَ الْمَوْلى وَلَبِئْسَ الْعَشِيرُ): the clause is a badal from the previous clause يدعو, so it amounts to a repetition of it and has no grammatical position. يدعو is an imperfect verb; the lām is of commencement (ibtidāʾ), or it prepares for an oath; من is a relative noun, a mubtadaʾ; ضره is a second mubtadaʾ, and أقرب من نفعه is the khabar of ضره; the clause ضره أقرب من نفعه is the ṣila of من, and the clause لبئس المولى is the khabar of من. An objection to this i'rab is the entry of the lām of commencement on the khabar, which is weak with respect to the grammatical rules — unless it is said that the lām was repeated for intensification. You may make يدعو one of the verbs of the heart, containing the sense of يزعم (claims), because يزعم is speech with belief; then the clause لمن ضره أقرب من نفعه is in the position of accusative as a mafʿūl bihi, because the lām of commencement suspends (the verb) from governing it. Or يدعو has the sense of يقول (says); then من is a mubtadaʾ, ضره a second mubtadaʾ and أقرب its khabar, the clause being the ṣila of من, and the khabar of من is omitted, its implied form being إله (a god) or إلهي (my god), and the position of the clause is accusative by the (verb of) saying. The clause لبئس is resumptive, because it cannot validly enter into the quoted speech, since the unbelievers do not say of their idols "how evil a patron and how evil a companion". There is another acceptable aspect, namely that the lām is redundant on the mafʿūl bihi of يدعو. This aspect is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd): يدعو من ضره, without the lām of commencement; so من is the object of يدعو, ضره is a mubtadaʾ and أقرب a khabar, and the clause is the ṣila of من. Al-Jalāl al-Suyūṭī chose this aspect, and his commentators supported it. As for al-Zamakhsharī, this is the text of his statement:
"The 'far straying' is borrowed from the straying of one who has gone far into the wilderness, lost, so that the distance of his straying grew long and far. If you say: harm and benefit are denied of the idols and affirmed of them in the two verses, and this is a contradiction? I say: once the meaning is grasped, this illusion goes away. That is, Allah the Exalted declared the unbeliever foolish in that he worships an inanimate thing that possesses neither harm nor benefit, while he believes of it, in his ignorance and straying, that he will seek its intercession when he seeks its intercession. Then He said: on the Day of Resurrection this unbeliever will say, with invocation and screaming, when he sees the harm he has incurred through the idols and his entering the Fire through worshipping them, and does not see any effect of the intercession he claimed for it: «لَمَنْ ضَرُّهُ أَقْرَبُ مِنْ نَفْعِهِ لَبِئْسَ الْمَوْلى وَلَبِئْسَ الْعَشِيرُ». Or He repeated يدعو, as though He said: he calls, he calls upon, besides Allah, what neither harms him nor benefits him; then He said: «لمن ضره» — by its being worshipped — «is nearer than its benefit» — by its being an intercessor — «how evil a patron». And in the reading (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh: من ضره, without a lām."
So it is as though al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, summarised the i'rab analyses we have cited, although there are numerous aspects that the commentators have followed, exceeding seven, but all of them are far from logic. We cite for you one of them by way of example, the view of al-Farrāʾ; he said: "The implied form is يدعو من لضره (he calls upon one whose harm…); then the lām was placed before its position." The arbitrariness in it is not hidden, as is the placing of what is in the ṣila of الذي before it.
There is a view no less strange and anomalous than this, namely that ذلك has the sense of الذي, in the position of accusative by يدعو, that is: he calls upon that which is the straying; but the object was fronted. This proceeds on the view of whoever makes ذا, without interrogation, have the sense of الذي, although it is confined to your saying ماذا and من ذا? And there is another, even more impossible, view, namely that the implied form is: ذلك هو الضلال البعيد يدعوه; so ذلك is a mubtadaʾ, هو a second mubtadaʾ, or a badal, or a pronoun of separation, الضلال the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, and يدعوه a ḥāl, the implied form being مدعوًّا (being called upon). It is an aspect that, as you see, condemns itself as feeble. We cited these views only to arrive at the statement that this verse is among the difficult passages that have occupied the scholars of grammar and exegesis, and they have not produced anything in it that quenches thirst; and the inimitable speech of Allah is too lofty to be reached by the rules that man has laid down.
بئس is an inflexible (jāmid) past verb for expressing blame; المولى is the agent, and the one specified for blame (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, its implied form being "it". ولبئس العشير is conjoined to His saying لبئس المولى.

dervis-irab:14-17.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْمَجُوسَ): المجوس (the Magi) was applied to a class of priests who had a momentous role in the ancient Iranian religion, especially in the Sasanian era, and the name was applied to classes of astrologers and learned men. The Magi are mentioned in the Gospel of Matthew: they were men of astronomy who were enlightened by a special revelation about the coming of Christ; they came from a region not far east of Palestine, as is supposed, guided by a star in the sky until they reached Bethlehem and presented their gifts to the infant Christ. Popular tradition has it that they were three and of royal lineage. The Arabs applied (the name) المجوس to the Norman and Scandinavian pirates who in the Middle Ages tried to storm the coasts and borders in the lands of the Islamic West. The scholars differed about the Magi: it is said they are a people who worship fire; it is said the sun; it is said they are those who hold that the world has two principles, light and darkness; and it is said they are a people who use impurities (النجاسات), the origin being نجوس, and the nūn was replaced by a mīm [Translator's note: the printed text says "the mīm was replaced by a nūn"; the derivation described requires the reverse]. The explanation of the words of this verse has preceded, except المجوس.

* I'rab:
(إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُدْخِلُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ جَنَّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهارُ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَفْعَلُ ما يُرِيدُ): إنّ with its noun, and the clause يدخل is the khabar (predicate); الذين is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); the clause عملوا الصالحات is conjoined to آمنوا. The sentence is resumptive, set out to establish the destiny of the believers who do righteous deeds. جنات is a second mafʿūl bihi by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa), or accusative by removal of the preposition (bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ); the clause تجري من تحتها الأنهار is a naʿt (adjective) of جنات. The clause إن الله يفعل ما يريد is resumptive, giving the reason for what preceded: إنّ with its noun, and the clause يفعل is the khabar; the agent of يفعل is latent, its implied form being "He"; ما is a mafʿūl bihi, and the clause يريد is the ṣila (relative clause).
(مَنْ كانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيا وَالْآخِرَةِ): من is conditional, a mubtadaʾ (subject); or relative, in which case the fāʾ in what follows links because of resemblance to the condition; the first is more likely. كان is a deficient past verb whose noun is latent, referring to من, and the clause يظن is the khabar; the agent of يظن is latent, referring to من. أن is lightened from the heavy (أنّ), its noun omitted, the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the clause لن ينصره الله is its khabar; أن and what follows it take the place of the two objects of يظن. في الدنيا is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) ينصره, and الآخرة is conjoined to الدنيا.
(فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ إِلَى السَّماءِ ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ فَلْيَنْظُرْ هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ ما يَغِيظُ): the fāʾ links the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ); the lām is the lām of command, and يمدد is an imperfect verb made jussive (majzūm) by the lām of command; the agent is latent, its implied form being "he"; بسبب is attached to يمدد; إلى السماء is a naʿt of سبب, and what is meant by السماء is the ceiling of the house. ثم ليقطع is conjoined to فليمدد. هل is an interrogative particle; يذهبن is an imperfect verb indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa; كيده is a mafʿūl bihi [Translator's note: as written; in the usual analysis كيده is the agent and ما the object], and ما يغيظ is the agent of يذهبن; the clause يغيظ is the ṣila; the clause هل يذهبن is in the position of accusative by ينظر. A full detailed account of this verse will come in the Rhetoric section.
(وَكَذلِكَ أَنْزَلْناهُ آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَنْ يُرِيدُ): the wāw is a conjunction; كذلك is a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun); أنزلناه is a verb, an agent and a mafʿūl bihi; آيات is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the hāʾ, and بينات is a naʿt. وأن الله is conjoined to the hāʾ of أنزلناه, the meaning being: and We sent down that Allah guides whomever He wills to guide. You may make the wāw circumstantial, and أنّ with what is in its scope in the position of nominative for an implied mubtadaʾ, that is: and the matter is that Allah guides whom He wills. أنّ with its noun, and the clause يهدي is its khabar; من is the object of يهدي, and the clause يريد is the ṣila of من.
(إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَالَّذِينَ هادُوا وَالصَّابِئِينَ وَالنَّصارى وَالْمَجُوسَ وَالَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا): إنّ with its noun; the clause آمنوا is the ṣila, and what follows is conjoined to الذين. The sentence is initial (ibtidāʾiyya).
(إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ): the second إنّ with its noun and khabar is in the position of nominative as the khabar of the first إنّ. The secret of opening the two clauses with إنّ will come. Or you make the second an emphasis (tawkīd) of the first, and His saying (إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ شَهِيدٌ) is the khabar: إنّ with its noun; على كل شيء is attached to شهيد, and شهيد is the khabar of إنّ. It is also said that the khabar is omitted, its implied form being "acknowledging" or the like, and what is mentioned is an explanation of it.

* Rhetoric:
1- Ījāz (concision) and tamthīl (allegory):
In the saying of the Exalted «مَنْ كانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ» up to His saying «ما يغيظ» there is ījāz and tamthīl. As for the ījāz, it is because its meaning is: whoever among the enviers and haters of Muḥammad thinks that Allah will not help him, and that He will do something other than helping; and whoever is enraged that Muḥammad attains what he seeks and reaches the lofty ideals he aimed at, which We have drawn for him, let him exhaust his capacity and spend all his effort; his likeness will be nothing but the likeness of one who takes a rope, stretches it to the ceiling of his house and strangles himself with it; then after all that let him look and reflect anew to see whether the help of Allah, which enrages him and robs him of sleep, has gone, and whether the burning and anguish that beset him have gone from him?
Strangling was called "cutting" (قطع) because the one who is strangled cuts his breath by blocking its passages; from this, breathlessness (البهر) was called القطع, and البهر is rapid succession of breath. Al-Jawharī said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "And the saying of the Exalted ثم ليقطع: they said, let him strangle himself, because the one who strangles himself stretches the rope to the ceiling, then cuts himself off from the ground until he is strangled. You say from it: قطع الرجل, that is, he was strangled; and لبن قاطع, that is, sour milk." I say: the common people use this expression for something whose goodness has gone and has worn out, and it is pure, eloquent Arabic. This act was called كيد (scheme) because He put it in its place, either because he is not able to do anything else and possesses nothing else, or by way of mockery. The commentators have expanded on this verse and taken it in various directions. They said: "It may be meant: let him stretch a rope to the overarching sky and climb up it, then cut off the revelation." Others said: "The help is provision; provisions are in the hand of Allah, not obtained except by His will, and the servant must be content with His apportionment; so whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for him, and has no patience or submission, let him reach the utmost limit of anguish, which is strangling, for that will not overturn the apportionment nor return him provided for." Other things have been said. What we have mentioned is more fitting and more complete for the intended meaning; it is what stirs within every envier, and what is said to everyone who objects to what is not within his capacity nor within the range of his will: you say to him, "Drink the sea," or "Kill yourself," for you have no means of changing what is an established reality, and the will of Allah is stronger.

2- Opening the two clauses with إنّ:
Opening the two clauses with إنّ adds emphasis to the speech, and the poets have looked to it in their poetry. Jarīr said:
إن الخليفة إن الله سربله ... سربال ملك به تزجى الخواتيم
(Truly the caliph — truly Allah has clothed him in the robe of kingship, by which the outcomes are driven.)
His saying إن الله سربله is the khabar of the first إنّ, and he repeated it to emphasise the emphasis. سربله: He clothed him with kingship, which resembles a robe (سربال); it is also narrated لباس ملك. His saying به: that is, by that garment or kingship; تزجى: that is, are driven; الخواتيم is the plural of خاتم, with fatḥa and kasra, the original being خواتم, and the yāʾ was added [Translator's note: the printed text says "the bāʾ was added"; the yāʾ is meant]; what is meant by it is praiseworthy outcomes of affairs and their ends. Abū Ḥayyān said: "It is possible that the khabar of إنّ is his saying به تزجى الخواتيم, and the clause إن الله سربله is parenthetical." It is also narrated ترجى, with the undotted rāʾ.

dervis-irab:47-53.t:
* I'rab:
(وَيَسْتَعْجِلُونَكَ بِالْعَذابِ وَلَنْ يُخْلِفَ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ) The wāw is a conjunction; (يستعجلونك) is an imperfect verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (بالعذاب) is a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) (يستعجلونك), i.e. they demand that you hasten it, by way of mockery. The wāw is a conjunction; (لن) is a particle of negation, of the accusative and of the future; (يخلف) is an imperfect verb, accusative (manṣūb) by (لن); (الله) is the fāʿil and (وعده) is the mafʿūl bihi. (وَإِنَّ يَوْماً عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ كَأَلْفِ سَنَةٍ مِمَّا تَعُدُّونَ) The wāw is for the ḥāl (circumstantial); (إن) and its noun; (عند ربك): the adverb is attached to an omitted ḥāl; the kāf is the khabar (predicate) of (إن); (مما) is a naʿt (adjective) of (سنة), and the clause (تعدون) is the ṣila (relative clause). In the comparison He confined Himself to "a thousand" because the thousand is the utmost number without repetition, and days of hardship are felt to be long, in the manner of the poet's saying:
فقصارهن مع الهموم طويلة ... وطوالهن مع السرور قصار
(The short ones among them, amid cares, are long; and the long ones among them, amid joy, are short.)
(وَكَأَيِّنْ مِنْ قَرْيَةٍ أَمْلَيْتُ لَها وَهِيَ ظالِمَةٌ ثُمَّ أَخَذْتُها وَإِلَيَّ الْمَصِيرُ) The wāw is a conjunction. Al-Zamakhsharī said in his Kashshāf: «If you ask: why was the first conjoined with the fāʾ and this one with the wāw? I answer: the first occurred as a badal (substitute) for His saying «فَكَيْفَ كانَ نَكِيرِ», whereas this one takes the ruling of the two clauses conjoined with the wāw, I mean His saying «وَلَنْ يُخْلِفَ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ» and «إِنَّ يَوْماً عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ كَأَلْفِ سَنَةٍ مِمَّا تَعُدُّونَ».» (كأين) is declarative (khabariyya), in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject); (من قرية) is in the position of the accusative as the tamyīz (specification) of (كأين); the clause (أمليت لها) is a naʿt of (قرية); the wāw is circumstantial; (هي) is a mubtadaʾ and (ظالمة) the khabar, and the clause is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl; (ثم أخذتها) is conjoined to (أمليت); (وإليّ): the wāw is a conjunction or circumstantial, (إليّ) is a fronted khabar and (المصير) a delayed mubtadaʾ. (قُلْ يا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنَّما أَنَا لَكُمْ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ) (يا) is a vocative particle; (أيها) is the one addressed (munādā), an intended indefinite, indeclinable (mabnī) on the ḍamma, in the position of the accusative by the vocative; the hāʾ is for drawing attention; (الناس) is a badal of (أي); (إنما) is the restraining and restrained particle (kāffa wa-makfūfa); (أنا) is a mubtadaʾ, (نذير) the khabar and (مبين) a naʿt. (فَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ وَرِزْقٌ كَرِيمٌ) The fāʾ is for branching off (tafrīʿiyya); (الذين) is a mubtadaʾ; the clause (آمنوا) is the ṣila; (عملوا) is conjoined to (آمنوا); (الصالحات) is the mafʿūl bihi; (لهم) is a fronted khabar and (مغفرة) a delayed mubtadaʾ; (رزق) is conjoined to (مغفرة) and (كريم) is a naʿt of (رزق); the clause (لهم مغفرة) is the khabar of (الذين). (وَالَّذِينَ سَعَوْا فِي آياتِنا مُعاجِزِينَ أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَحِيمِ) The wāw is a conjunction; (الذين) is a mubtadaʾ; the clause (سعوا) is the ṣila; (في آياتنا) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (سعوا). The meaning of striving against the signs is corrupting them, falsifying them and nullifying them; one says "I strove in so-and-so's affair" when you set it right or spoiled it by this striving. (معاجزين) is a ḥāl, i.e. racing [to outstrip] in their claim and estimation: their souls had enticed them into thinking they could nullify the signs and turn people away from following them; so the form mufāʿala is not devoid of the meaning of supposition and belief with respect to them. (أولئك) is a mubtadaʾ and (أصحاب الجحيم) its khabar, and the clause is the khabar of (الذين). (وَما أَرْسَلْنا مِنْ قَبْلِكَ مِنْ رَسُولٍ وَلا نَبِيٍّ إِلَّا إِذا تَمَنَّى أَلْقَى الشَّيْطانُ فِي أُمْنِيَّتِهِ) The wāw is resumptive and the clause is resumptive, brought to begin a second consolation for the Prophet ﷺ. (ما) is negative; (أرسلنا) is a verb and its fāʿil; (من قبلك) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (أرسلنا), and (من) is for the beginning of the extent; (من رسول): (من) is redundant (zāʾida), and (رسول) is genitive in form and accusative in position as the mafʿūl bihi of (أرسلنا); (ولا نبي) is conjoined to (من رسول); (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (إذا) is an adverb of future time; the clause (تمنى) is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's annexation [to it]; the clause (ألقى الشيطان) has no grammatical position. The conditional sentence after (إلا) admits several aspects, the most preferable being that it is in the position of the genitive as a naʿt of (رسول) according to its form, and of the accusative according to the meaning; it may also be a ḥāl; and you may make the exception discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ), so that (إلا) is a particle of exception and the clause is in the accusative as the excepted. (في أمنيته) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (ألقى). The meaning of this "casting" and the story of the occasion of revelation will come in the Benefits section. Abū Ḥayyān found it problematic that a clause outwardly conditional, namely (إذا تمنى ألقى), should come after (إلا), and he answered that (إذا) has been stripped down to mere adverbial meaning with no condition in it, and that it separates (إلا) from the verb (ألقى), which is a permissible separation; so (إلا) is followed, in the underlying estimate, by a past verb, and a condition [for this] obtains, namely the occurrence of a verb before (إلا), which is (أرسلنا). Ibn Hishām said: What appears is that [the problem] only arises when (إلا) is followed by the verb itself in its wording, and this did not occur in the verse; so there is no problem and no need to interpret (إذا) as having departed from conditionality.
(فَيَنْسَخُ اللَّهُ ما يُلْقِي الشَّيْطانُ ثُمَّ يُحْكِمُ اللَّهُ آياتِهِ وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ) The fāʾ is resumptive; (ينسخ الله) is an imperfect verb and its fāʿil; (ما) is the mafʿūl bihi; the clause (يلقي الشيطان) is the ṣila; (ثم) is a conjunction; (يحكم الله) is a verb and its fāʿil and (آياته) the mafʿūl bihi; (والله عليم حكيم) is a parenthetical clause composed of a mubtadaʾ and its two khabars.
(لِيَجْعَلَ ما يُلْقِي الشَّيْطانُ فِتْنَةً لِلَّذِينَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ وَالْقاسِيَةِ قُلُوبُهُمْ) The lām is causal and the verb after it is accusative by an implied (أن); it [the lām and what follows] is attached to (يحكم), i.e. then Allah makes His signs firm in order to make…; it may also be attached to (ينسخ). (ما) is relative or maṣdariyya, and in either case it is the first mafʿūl bihi; the clause (يلقي الشيطان) is the ṣila; (فتنة) is the second mafʿūl bihi; (للذين) is a naʿt of (فتنة); (في قلوبهم) is a fronted khabar and (مرض) a delayed mubtadaʾ, and the clause is the ṣila of (الذين); (القاسية) is conjoined to (الذين), and (قلوبهم) is the fāʿil of (القاسية). It is useful to mention that the (ال) in (القاسية) is relative and (القاسية) is its ṣila [Translator's note: the Arabic says «صفتها», literally "its adjective", i.e. the participle serving as the content of the relative al-]; it is made feminine because what it puts in the nominative, namely (قلوبهم), is figuratively feminine. (وَإِنَّ الظَّالِمِينَ لَفِي شِقاقٍ بَعِيدٍ) The wāw is circumstantial or resumptive; (إن) and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); (في شقاق) is its khabar and (بعيد) a naʿt of (شقاق).

The legend of the Gharānīq (the "high cranes"):
We now turn to a question that has occupied Muslim scholars in ancient and modern times and has claimed the attention of many of them because of its gravity and the weight of the matters it involves, which a researcher may not pass over like a hurried rider; for it touches the essence of the creed and concerns the infallibility (ʿiṣma) of the bearer of the message. To speak about it carelessly, without careful reflection and sifting, is in no way permissible. We shall first narrate the legend as it is, with its defects, as the exegetes transmitted it, without refuting it or raising doubts about it. It was transmitted so widely that it became evening talk with which people amuse themselves and pass their idle time, and people by nature incline to everything strange. This is the legend:
When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw his people turning away from him because he faulted their idols and disparaged their gods, he became weary of this turning away; and because of his eagerness for their Islam and his devotion to it, he wished that nothing would be revealed to him that would repel them, hoping he might take that as a way to win them over and bring them down from their error and obstinacy. That wish stayed with him until the sūra «وَالنَّجْمِ إِذا هَوى» was revealed to him while he was in his people's assembly, with that wish in his soul. He began to recite it, and when he reached His saying «وَمَناةَ الثَّالِثَةَ الْأُخْرى», «أَلْقَى الشَّيْطانُ فِي أُمْنِيَّتِهِ», the wish he had wished, by whispering to him what accompanied it, so that his tongue ran ahead, by way of inadvertence and error, until he said: "Those are the exalted Gharānīq, and their intercession is indeed hoped for" (it is also narrated as "al-gharāniqa"). He did not notice it until infallibility overtook him and he became aware of it; it is also said that Gabriel, peace be upon him, alerted him; or [it is said] that Satan spoke those words and made the people hear them. When he prostrated at its end, everyone in the assembly prostrated with him and they were pleased. Satan's being enabled to do this was a trial from Allah and a test by which the hypocrites increased in doubt and darkness and the believers in light and certainty.
What follows is a selection of the statements of the scholars and exegetes. Al-Rāzī said, in summary: This story is not established by way of transmission. Then he discussed how the narrators of this story are impugned. Moreover, al-Bukhārī narrated in his Ṣaḥīḥ that he, upon him be blessings and peace, recited Sūrat al-Najm and the Muslims, the polytheists, men and jinn prostrated with him, and the account of the Gharānīq is not in it; rather this ḥadīth has been narrated by many routes and the account of the Gharānīq is not in any of them at all. There is no doubt that whoever deems it possible that the Messenger glorified idols has disbelieved, because it is known by necessity that his greatest effort was in negating idols. Were we to allow that, security would be removed from his law, and we would allow that every one of the rulings and laws might be like that, i.e. something Satan cast onto his tongue, and His saying, Exalted is He, «يا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ ما أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ وَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ فَما بَلَّغْتَ رِسالَتَهُ» would be voided, for to reason there is no difference between subtracting from revelation and adding to it. By these transmitted and rational considerations we know, in general terms, that this story is fabricated; and it has been said that this story was fabricated by the zanādiqa (heretics) and has no basis. End of al-Rāzī's words.
As for Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, the commentator on al-Bukhārī, he pointed out in Fatḥ al-Bārī on al-Bukhārī that it has an established basis, and he said, may Allah forgive him: «Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarī and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted by routes from Shuʿba, from Abū Bishr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited al-Najm in Mecca, and when he reached «أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ اللَّاتَ وَالْعُزَّى، وَمَناةَ الثَّالِثَةَ الْأُخْرى», Satan cast onto his tongue: "Those are the exalted Gharānīq, and their intercession is indeed hoped for." The polytheists said: He has never mentioned our gods favourably before today. When he finished the sūra he prostrated and they prostrated. That weighed heavily on the Prophet, so there was revealed in consolation of him «وَما أَرْسَلْنا مِنْ قَبْلِكَ مِنْ رَسُولٍ وَلا نَبِيٍّ إِلَّا إِذا تَمَنَّى أَلْقَى الشَّيْطانُ فِي أُمْنِيَّتِهِ», i.e. in his recitation, between his words.
Al-Bazzār and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it by way of Umayya ibn Khālid from Shuʿba, and he said in its chain: from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, as I reckon; then he cited the aforementioned ḥadīth. Al-Bazzār said: It is narrated as connected only with this chain, and Umayya ibn Khālid alone connected it, and he is reliable and well known.
Al-Ṭabarī cited it by way of al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās. The meaning in all of them is one. Every route of it other than that of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is either weak or broken; but the multitude of routes indicates that the story has a basis, in addition to which it has two other mursal (disconnected at the Companion level) routes whose men meet the conditions of the ṣaḥīḥ: one of them is what al-Ṭabarī transmitted by way of Yūnus ibn Zayd from Ibn Shihāb: Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām narrated to me, and he mentioned something similar; and the second is what he transmitted by way of al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān and Ḥammād ibn Salama, both from Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, from Abū al-ʿĀliya.»
And Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī said in the course of his rebuttal of al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī: «Ibn al-ʿArabī was audacious, as is his habit, and said: al-Ṭabarī mentioned on this many narrations that have no basis. This is an unqualified statement that is rejected. Likewise the statement of al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ: This ḥadīth was not transmitted by the people of soundness, nor by any reliable narrator with a sound connected chain, besides the weakness of its transmitters, the disorder of its narrations and the breaks in its chains. Likewise the statement of ʿIyāḍ also: None of the Successors and exegetes from whom this story is related gave it a chain or traced it back to a Companion, and most of the routes from them on this are weak and flimsy. This too is rejected.»
The rest of al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ's words shows how free he was from the bane of blind imitation and how he tried to sift the facts. He said: «Al-Bazzār [Translator's note: the text spells it «البزاز»] made clear that the ḥadīth is not known by any route that may be mentioned except by way of Abū Bishr from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, with the doubt that occurred about its being connected; as for al-Kalbī, narrating from him is not permissible because of the severity of his weakness. Then he rejected it by way of reasoning: had that happened, many of those who had accepted Islam would have apostatised. He said: And that has not been reported.»
Al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar said: «All of that does not accord with the rules of the ḥadīth scholars, for when routes are many and their points of origin differ, that indicates that it has a basis. We have mentioned that three of its chains meet the conditions of the ṣaḥīḥ, and they are mursal reports of the kind used as proof by those who accept the mursal as proof, and likewise by those who do not, since they support one another. Once that is established, it is necessary to interpret what objectionable content occurs in them, namely his saying: Satan cast onto his tongue "Those are the exalted Gharānīq, and their intercession is indeed hoped for"; for it is not permissible to take that at face value, because it is impossible for him ﷺ to add to the Qur'an deliberately what is not in it, and likewise inadvertently, since it contradicts the monotheism he brought, on account of his infallibility.» He went on to say: «The scholars have taken some seven paths in interpreting this. It was said that it ran on his tongue when a light doze overtook him and he was unaware; and when Allah informed him of that, He made His signs firm. Al-Ṭabarī transmitted this from Qatāda.»
Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ rejected it on the ground that it is not sound, since that is not possible for the Prophet, and Satan has no authority over him in sleep.
It was said: Satan forced him to say that without choice. Ibn al-ʿArabī rejected this by His saying, Exalted is He, relating Satan's words: «وَما كانَ لِي عَلَيْكُمْ مِنْ سُلْطانٍ ... الآية». He said: If Satan had power for that, no one would be left with power for obedience.
It was said: When the polytheists mentioned their gods they used to describe them thus, and that stuck in his ﷺ memory and ran on his tongue inadvertently. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ rejected that, and did it excellently.
It was said: Perhaps he said it as a rebuke to the disbelievers. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said: This is permissible if there was a contextual indication pointing to what was intended, especially since speaking during prayer was permissible at that time. Al-Bāqillānī inclined to this.
It was said: When he reached His saying «وَمَناةَ الثَّالِثَةَ الْأُخْرى», the polytheists feared that he would bring after it something by which he would disparage their gods, as was his habit when he mentioned them, so they hastened to those words and mixed them into the Prophet's ﷺ recitation, following their habit in their saying «لا تَسْمَعُوا لِهذَا الْقُرْآنِ وَالْغَوْا فِيهِ», i.e. make idle noise by raising voices to confuse and disturb him; and that was attributed to Satan because he was the one who drove them to it, or what is meant by Satan is a human devil.
It was said: What is meant by "the exalted Gharānīq" is the angels. The disbelievers used to say:
"The angels are the daughters of Allah", and they worshipped them. So he mentioned all of them in sequence in order to refute them by His saying «أَلَكُمُ الذَّكَرُ وَلَهُ الْأُنْثى». When the polytheists heard it, they applied it to all of them and said: He has glorified our gods, and they were pleased with that. So He abrogated those two phrases, namely: "Those are the exalted Gharānīq, and their intercession is indeed hoped for", and made His signs firm.
It was said: The Prophet ﷺ was reciting the Qur'an in measured tones, and Satan lay in wait for him at one of his pauses and uttered those words imitating the voice of the Prophet ﷺ, so that whoever was near him heard it, thought it was the Prophet's speech and spread it. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said: This is the best of the aspects, and it is the one whose preponderance appears; it is supported by what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās in explaining (تمنى) as "recited". Ibn al-ʿArabī likewise approved this interpretation and said: The meaning of His saying (في أمنيته) is "in his recitation". So the Exalted informed in this verse that Allah's way with His messengers is that when they said something, Satan added to it on his own account; this is an explicit text that Satan added to the speech of the Prophet ﷺ, that the Prophet ﷺ said it, because he is infallible. [Translator's note: so in the source; the sense of Ibn al-ʿArabī's argument requires "not that the Prophet ﷺ said it", and a negative particle appears to have dropped out.]
He said in Fatḥ al-Bārī: «Al-Ṭabarī, with his eminent standing, vast knowledge and strong ability in reasoning, preceded [them] in this and judged this meaning to be correct.» End.
As for what has come in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī concerning this story [Translator's note: the text reads «ما ما ورد», evidently for «أما ما ورد»], it is: «Ibn ʿAbbās said about «إِذا تَمَنَّى أَلْقَى الشَّيْطانُ فِي أُمْنِيَّتِهِ»: When he spoke, Satan cast into his speech, and Allah nullifies what Satan casts and makes His signs firm. And it is said: his umniyya is his recitation: «الأماني يقرءون ولا يكتبون» (al-amānī: they recite and do not write).» So you see that he related the explanation of umniyya as recitation with the wording "it is said", after he had explained it as speech in a narration from Ibn ʿAbbās; this indicates a difference between the two explanations. So what the commentators claim, that "speech" in Ibn ʿAbbās's view means recitation, contradicts the apparent sense of the wording; moreover his relating the explanation of umniyya in the sense of recitation with the wording "it is said" conveys that it is not authoritative in his view. It will come that what is meant by "speech" is the speech of the soul [i.e. inner thought].
Al-Qasṭallānī said in his commentary on al-Bukhārī: «More than one of the imams has impugned this story, so that Ibn Isḥāq said, when asked about it: It is a fabrication of the zanādiqa.» It suffices for rejecting a ḥadīth that Ibn Isḥāq should say about it that it is a fabrication of the zanādiqa, given Ibn Isḥāq's standing known among the ḥadīth scholars.
This is the text of what al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said: «What has come in the ṣaḥīḥ is that the Prophet ﷺ recited al-Najm while in Mecca, and the Muslims, the polytheists, jinn and men prostrated with him; that may have been due to the eloquence of the sūra, the force of its impact and the magnitude of its effect.» Then al-Qāḍī said: «The proof has been established and the Community has agreed upon his ﷺ infallibility and his being free from this vice.»
[That is:] either that he wished that something like this, praise of gods other than Allah, which is disbelief, should be revealed to him; or that Satan should gain mastery over him and confuse the Qur'an for him so that he puts into it what is not of it, and the Prophet ﷺ believes that something not of the Qur'an is of it, until Gabriel, peace be upon him, makes him understand; all of that is impossible in his ﷺ case; or that the Prophet ﷺ should say that of his own accord, deliberately, which is disbelief, or inadvertently, and he is protected from all of this. We have established by proofs and consensus his ﷺ protection from disbelief running on his tongue or in his heart, whether deliberately or inadvertently; or that what the angel conveys should be confused for him with what Satan casts; or that Satan should have a way over him; or that he should falsely attribute to Allah, neither deliberately nor inadvertently, what was not revealed to him. Allah the Exalted has said: «وَلَوْ تَقَوَّلَ عَلَيْنا بَعْضَ الْأَقاوِيلِ لَأَخَذْنا مِنْهُ بِالْيَمِينِ ثُمَّ لَقَطَعْنا مِنْهُ الْوَتِينَ», and He said: «إِذاً لَأَذَقْناكَ ضِعْفَ الْحَياةِ وَضِعْفَ الْمَماتِ ثُمَّ لا تَجِدُ لَكَ عَلَيْنا نَصِيراً». [Translator's note: the opening «أما من تمنيه» of this paragraph appears to be garbled in the source; it continues ʿIyāḍ's list of what the Prophet ﷺ is free from, and is translated here in that sense.]
A second aspect is the impossibility of this story by reasoning and by custom: had these words been as narrated, they would have been ill-fitting, self-contradictory in their parts, mixing praise with blame, and disjointed in composition and arrangement; and neither the Prophet ﷺ nor the Muslims present with him nor the chiefs of the polytheists were people from whom that could be hidden. This would not be hidden from the least reflective person, so how from one whose forbearance was weighty and whose knowledge was wide in eloquence and in recognising pure speech?
A third aspect: it is known of the habit of the hypocrites, the obstinacy of the polytheists, and the weak-hearted and ignorant among the Muslims, that they recoil at the first instant; that the enemy would confuse matters against the Prophet ﷺ at the slightest trial; that they would revile the Muslims and gloat over them time after time; and that those with sickness in their hearts among those who professed Islam would apostatise at the least doubt. Yet no one has related anything in this story other than this narration, weak in its basis. Had it happened, Quraysh would have found in it an assault upon the Muslims, and the Jews would have established a proof against them, as they did, out of stubbornness, in the story of the Night Journey. No trial would have been greater than this affliction had it existed, and no stirring of trouble by an enemy would then have been more severe than this incident had it been possible; yet not a word about it has come from an opponent, nor a syllable from a Muslim because of it. This shows its falsity and the uprooting of its basis. There is no doubt that some devils of men and jinn inserted this ḥadīth among some heedless ḥadīth transmitters, in order to confuse some weak Muslims with it.
A fourth aspect: The narrators of this story mention that concerning it was revealed: «وَإِنْ كادُوا لَيَفْتِنُونَكَ عَنِ الَّذِي أَوْحَيْنا إِلَيْكَ», the two verses. These two verses refute the report they narrated, because Allah the Exalted mentioned that they nearly tempted him so that he would fabricate, and that had He not made him firm he would nearly have inclined to them a little. The content and implied sense of this is that Allah protected him from fabricating and made him firm so that he did not incline to them even a little, so how much? Yet they narrate in their flimsy reports that he went beyond inclining and fabricating, to praising their gods, and that he ﷺ said: I fabricated against Allah and said what He did not say. This would weaken the ḥadīth even if it were sound, so how when it has no soundness? This is like His saying, Exalted is He, in the other verse: «وَلَوْلا فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ وَرَحْمَتُهُ لَهَمَّتْ طائِفَةٌ مِنْهُمْ أَنْ يُضِلُّوكَ وَما يُضِلُّونَ إِلَّا أَنْفُسَهُمْ وَما يَضُرُّونَكَ مِنْ شَيْءٍ».
Al-Qushayrī said: Quraysh and Thaqīf demanded of him, when he passed by their gods, that he turn his face towards them, and promised him faith in him if he did so; but he did not do it, nor would he have done it. Ibn al-Anbārī said:
«The Messenger neither came near nor inclined.»
As for what Ibn Ḥajar mentioned, that the story was narrated mursal by three routes meeting the conditions of the ṣaḥīḥ and that it is used as proof, etc., as preceded, it escaped him that infallibility is among the doctrines in which certainty is required; so a ḥadīth that conveys its breach and violation is not accepted in whatever way it comes. The legal theorists have counted a report of this description among the reports whose falsity must be affirmed with certainty. That is if the ḥadīth were supposed connected, so what do you think of mursal reports? The disagreement about using the mursal as proof or not concerns only matters of practice and the branches of rulings, not the foundations of creed and the cardinal points of faith in the messengers and what they brought. So it is a slip of Ibn Ḥajar, may Allah forgive him for it. Brockelmann, the famous German orientalist, exploited this narration, transmitted it faithfully and considered it one of the questions settled beyond proof, in his book "History of the Islamic Peoples", which he brought out in 1939 CE. Speaking of Muḥammad he said: «But it seems that in the first years of his mission he acknowledged the three goddesses of the Kaʿba, whom his fellow citizens considered the daughters of Allah, and he alluded to them in one of the verses revealed to him with his words:
"Those are the exalted Gharānīq, and their intercession is hoped for." Afterwards, however, when the Prophet's sense of oneness grew stronger, he acknowledged no intercessors with Allah other than the angels; and the fifty-third sūra came, containing a denial that the three goddesses are the daughters of Allah. Later tradition could regard that concession only as a deviation into which Satan had tempted him, and therefore its events were postponed to the most straitened times in Mecca; then he soon denied it and disowned it the next day.» This is what Brockelmann mentioned; it oozes with bigotry and proclaims its own fabrication. The matter was not confined to Brockelmann alone: many missionaries and some orientalists clung to this narration and claimed that the Messenger did that when the polytheists resisted him in Mecca, wishing to draw close to them, so he praised their gods; then they counted this act of his as a slackening of his strictness in monotheism and his attack on the idols. Many Muslim scholars in the modern age have confronted them, refuted their fabrications and cast away their rumours. It suffices us to point to two of the great among these scholars, summarising what they said and turning away from lengthiness that does not accord with the method of this book.

Summary of what the Indian scholar Muḥammad ʿAlī wrote:
«This narration is found in al-Wāqidī and al-Ṭabarī, yet it has no shadow of truth, for every one of the deeds of the Messenger of Allah contradicts such a tendency. Add to that that al-Wāqidī is known for narrating isrāʾīliyyāt and legends, and likewise al-Ṭabarī is known for amassing much and exhausting the narrations whatever their share of soundness. Moreover, if we turn to the narration of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq or to Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, which left nothing of the Messenger's life unmentioned, we see no trace of the Gharānīq story. Ibn Isḥāq came forty years before al-Wāqidī and about a hundred and fifty years or more before al-Ṭabarī; as for al-Bukhārī, he was a contemporary of al-Wāqidī, yet he did not mention this story. Further, al-Wāqidī is known among the ḥadīth scholars to fabricate ḥadīths and to be unreliable in what he narrates; and likewise none of the ḥadīth narrators mentioned it.
If we return to reading the verses themselves in sequence, we find them: «أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ اللَّاتَ وَالْعُزَّى وَمَناةَ الثَّالِثَةَ الْأُخْرى، أَلَكُمُ الذَّكَرُ وَلَهُ الْأُنْثى؟ تِلْكَ إِذاً قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزى، إِنْ هِيَ إِلَّا أَسْماءٌ سَمَّيْتُمُوها أَنْتُمْ وَآباؤُكُمْ ما أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ بِها مِنْ سُلْطانٍ، إِنْ يَتَّبِعُونَ إِلَّا الظَّنَّ وَما تَهْوَى الْأَنْفُسُ، وَلَقَدْ جاءَهُمْ مِنْ رَبِّهِمُ الْهُدى». It is not reasonable that a verse contradicting them in the foundation of the Islamic creed and the core of Muḥammad's ﷺ call should be crammed among these successive verses. There are many further details in refuting this narration that are of no use to mention.»
This is what the Indian scholar Mawlānā Muḥammad ʿAlī mentioned, and it suffices as a reply to these orientalists who look at Muḥammad's prophethood with a materialistic view stripped of divine inspiration. That is nothing but religious bigotry built on political enmity: they deny that Muḥammad had a genuine prophethood while they acknowledge this very prophethood for all the prophets of the Children of Israel.

Summary of the eminent study written by the Imām Muḥammad ʿAbduh:
Now it is time for us to summarise the delightful study written by the Imām Shaykh Muḥammad ʿAbduh, in which "Juhayza cut off the speech of every orator" [a proverb: it settled the matter]:
«It is not hidden from anyone who understands Arabic and has read something of the Qur'an that His saying, Exalted is He, «وَما أَرْسَلْنا مِنْ قَبْلِكَ مِنْ رَسُولٍ وَلا نَبِيٍّ ... الآيات» relates a decree decreed for all the messengers, which they do not exceed and do not stop short of, and describes a familiar trait known among them and their nations. If what those exegetes said were sound, the meaning would be that Satan was given power over all the prophets and messengers and mixed up the revelation sent down to them, but after this mixing Allah abrogates Satan's speech and makes His signs firm. This is among the ugliest things anyone could imagine regarding Allah the Exalted's singling out His prophets and choosing them from the elite of His friends. So let us leave this raving and return to what we are about.» After the Master Imām had expounded at length on Allah's mentioning to His Prophet the states of the prophets and messengers before him, to show him His way with them, and that none of them was sent to a nation without having adversaries who harmed him by misinterpretation and distortion, he said: «So it is according to this meaning, which agrees with what all the prophets met, that the verse must be explained, and that is in two ways:

The first:
That (تمنى) means "recited" and (الأمنية) means recitation. This is a meaning that may be sound, and the word has been used in it. Ḥassān ibn Thābit said about ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with them both:
تمنى كتاب الله أول ليلة ... وآخره لاقى حمام المقادر
(He recited the Book of Allah at the start of the night, and at its end he met the death of the decrees.)
However, the "casting" is not in the sense they mentioned, but in the sense understood from your saying "I cast into so-and-so's speech" when you insert into it what its wording might bear but he did not intend, or attribute to him what he did not say on the pretext that his said speech leads to it. That is the work of the "مُعاجِزِين" who set themselves up to fight the truth, follow the doubtful, and pursue suspicion; casting in this sense is their custom. The casting is attributed to Satan because he is the stirrer of doubts by his whisperings and the corrupter of hearts by his intrigues, and everything that issues from the people of misguidance is attributed to him. The meaning then is: We sent no messenger or prophet before you but that, when he spoke to his people about his Lord or recited a revelation sent down to him containing guidance for them, troublemakers rose up in his face, turning what he recited to them away from its intended meaning, attributing to him what he did not say, and spreading that among people in order to keep them away from him and divert them from his path; then Allah establishes the truth and nullifies falsehood. The prophets continued to bear patiently being denied and harmed, striving in the truth, paying no heed to the attempts of those who would frustrate them nor to the mockery of the mockers, until the truth appears through striving and triumphs over falsehood through combat; then Allah abrogates that doubt, uproots it from its roots, and makes His signs firm and establishes them. Allah has set this way among people so that the foul may be distinguished from the good: those in whose hearts is sickness, the weak-minded, are tempted by those doubts and whisperings and run after them; and those whose hearts are hardened, the people of obstinacy and denial, are tempted by them and take them as a support they rely on in their disputation; then the truth is purified for those who have been given knowledge and becomes clear to them after every doubt has come upon it, so they know that it is the truth from your Lord and believe in it, and their hearts humble themselves and become tranquil. Those given knowledge are those granted the power to distinguish between the decisive proof by which the mind settles in the depth of certainty and the fallacies and kinds of sophistry that make understanding reckless, fly off with it into fancy, and take the mind now to the left and now to the right.

The second:
That (التمني) is in its well-known meaning, and likewise (الأمنية), which is of the pattern ufʿūla meaning "wish" (al-munya), its plural being amānī, as is well known. Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā said:
Tamannī is the soul's talk of what may be and what may not be; and tamannī is asking the Lord. In the ḥadīth: "When one of you wishes, let him ask for much, for he is only asking his Lord", and in a narration: "let him multiply". Ibn al-Athīr said: Tamannī is desiring the attainment of the thing wished for, and the soul's talk of what may be and what may not be. Abū Bakr said: "I wished for the thing" when you estimated it and loved that it become yours. All that has been said about the meaning of tamannī in this way goes back to what we mentioned, and the meaning of umniyya follows it. Allah has sent no messenger or prophet to call a people to new guidance or to a previous law He had legislated for them, and to bring them to believe in a book that he himself brought if he was a messenger, or that someone else [Translator's note: the text has «عيره», evidently a misprint for «غيره»] brought if he was a prophet sent to bring people to follow the one who preceded him, without his having a wish concerning his people, namely that they follow him, side with what he calls them to, seek healing from their disease by his remedy, and disobey their desires by answering his call. No messenger was sent but that he was more eager for his nation's faith and their belief in his message than for the food he ate, the drink he drank and the dwelling in which he found rest, from which he went out in the morning and to which he returned in the evening. Our Prophet ﷺ was at the highest station and loftiest place in this. Allah the Exalted said: «فَلَعَلَّكَ باخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ عَلى آثارِهِمْ إِنْ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهذَا الْحَدِيثِ أَسَفاً», and He said: «وما أكثر الناس ولو حرصت بمؤمنين», and He said: «أفأنت تكره الناس حتى يكونوا مؤمنين»; and in the verses there is much, too long to list, indicating his ﷺ wishes concerning the guidance of his people and bringing them out of the darknesses they were in to the light of what he brought. And no messenger or prophet, when he wished this lofty wish, but Satan cast stumbling blocks in his path, set up obstacles between him and his aim, whispered in people's breasts and robbed them of benefiting from the power of reason and perception they had been given; so they rose up against him, barred him from his aim and tried to frustrate him, until they sometimes did frustrate him, and disputed with him by word and weapon, until they sometimes overpowered him. When they prevailed over him while the call was at its beginning, and harming him was easy for them because his followers were few and his helpers weak, they thought the truth was on their side, and the obstacles they had cast between him and what he aimed at were a trial for them. Allah's way has prevailed that the messengers be from the middle ranks of their people or from the weak among them, so that what brings about submission to the truth is pure evidence and the force of proof, and so that absolute choice is what carries the one invited to it to accept it, and so that the truth does not share with falsehood in its means. Those who share in setting falsehood's snares and nets, the supporters of falsehood in every age, are the people of power, disdain and rank, of pride in wealth, children, clan and helpers, of delusion by ornaments and of vanity in many acquaintances. These traits gather, all or some of them, only in leaders and people of standing, so they distract them from themselves and turn their gaze from the path of their right guidance. When a caller calls to the truth, hearts pure of the filth of these temptations recognise it, and souls that are clear and minds ready to accept it, being free of these preoccupations, hasten to it; and these are rarely found except among the weak and the people of poverty. When these gather around the caller and back him in his call, those deluded ones rise up saying: «ما نراك إلا بشرا مثلنا وما نراك اتبعك إلا الذين هم أراذلنا بادي الرأي وما نرى لكم علينا من فضل بل نظنكم كاذبين». When Allah leads them on step by step according to His way, and makes the dispute between them and the believers alternate, those of their partisans in whose hearts is sickness are tempted, and they are tempted by the victory they gained in their defence. But Allah prevails over His affair: He obliterates what Satan has cast of these doubts, removes these impediments and those obstacles, grants authority to His signs, makes them firm and establishes their pillars, brings forth from the weakness of their supporters strength and replaces their humiliation with honour, and the word of Allah is the highest and the word of Satan the lowest: «فأما الزبد فيذهب جفاء وأما ما ينفع الناس فيمكث في الأرض».

An important conclusion by the Master Imām:
«If what the transmitters of the Gharānīq story said were sound, trust in revelation would be removed and reliance on it would collapse, as al-Bayḍāwī and others said; the abrogating text would be like the abrogated, in that Satan could cast into it whatever he wished; and the greatest pillar of the divine laws, namely infallibility, would be demolished. What is offered as a way out of this is repugnant to taste and is not considered by reason. Moreover, the Arabs' describing their gods as "the exalted Gharānīq" has not come either in their poetry or in their orations, and it has not been reported from anyone that this description was current on their tongues, except what came in Yāqūt's Muʿjam, without chain and not known by a sound route. This indicates that the story is an invention of the zanādiqa, as Ibn Isḥāq said, and it may have been the source of what Yāqūt cited. It is not hidden that al-ghurnūq and al-ghirnīq were known in the language only as the name of a black or white water bird, or it is the name of the crane or a bird resembling it; and al-ghurnīq with ḍamma, on the patterns of zunbūr, qindīl, samawʾal, firdaws, qirṭās and ʿulābiṭ, means a fair, handsome youth; a twisted lock of hair is called al-ghurnūq, as is a kind of tree; and al-ghurnūq and al-gharāniq are applied to the soft growth at the base of the boxthorn; and one says "a lock (lumma) gharāniqa and gharāniqiyya", i.e. soft, lit up by the wind, or al-ghurnūq is soft, hidden vegetation, etc. [Translator's note: the source has «ولا يقال لمة غرانقة», "it is not said", which seems to be a misprint for «ويقال», "it is said".] None of these meanings suits deities [Translator's note: the text has «الإلهام», "inspiration", evidently a misprint for «الآلهة», "deities"] and idols so as to be applied to them in eloquent speech presented to the kings of rhetoric and the princes of discourse.
